## Problem 1: Vectorization

1.
```{r}

fun1 <- function(n = 100, k = 4, lambda = 4) {
  x <- NULL
  
  for (i in 1:n){
    x <- rbind(x, rpois(k, lambda))    
  }
  
  return(x)
}

fun1alt <- function(n = 100, k = 4, lambda = 4) {
  matrix(rpois(n * k, lambda), nrow = n, ncol = k, byrow = TRUE)
}

set.seed(123)
x_slow <- fun1(n = 10000, k = 4, lambda = 4)

set.seed(123)
x_fast <- fun1alt(n = 10000, k = 4, lambda = 4)


identical(dim(x_slow), dim(x_fast))


comparison <- data.frame(
  Function = c("fun1", "fun1alt"),
  Mean = c(mean(x_slow), mean(x_fast)),
  Median = c(median(x_slow), median(x_fast)),
  Variance = c(var(as.vector(x_slow)),
               var(as.vector(x_fast)))
)

comparison
```
The two functions produced the same exact output, as shown.


```{r}

library(microbenchmark)
# Benchmarking
microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  fun1(),
  fun1alt()
)
```

However, fun1alt processed much faster than fun1 for every value except max.

```{r}

library(matrixStats)
# Data Generating Process (10 x 10,000 matrix)
set.seed(1234)
x <- matrix(rnorm(1e4), nrow = 10)

# Find each column's max value
fun2 <- function(x) {
  apply(x, 2, max)
}

fun2alt <- function(x) {
  matrixStats::colMaxs(x)
}

x_slow2 <- fun2(x)
x_fast2 <- fun2alt(x)

identical(x_slow2, x_fast2)

comparison2 <- data.frame(
  Function = c("fun2", "fun2alt"),
  Mean = c(mean(x_slow2), mean(x_fast2)), Median = c(median(x_slow2),median(x_fast2)),
  Variance = c(var(as.vector(x_slow2)),
               var(as.vector(x_fast2)))
)

comparison2

# Benchmarking
microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  fun2(x),
  fun2alt(x)
)
```

The two functions produced the same exact output, as shown. However, fun2alt processed much faster than fun2 for every value.


## Problem 3: Parallelization

```{r}
my_boot <- function(dat, stat, R, ncpus = 1L) {
  
  # Get the random indices
  n <- nrow(dat)
  idx <- matrix(
    sample.int(n, n * R, replace = TRUE),
    nrow = n,
    ncol = R
  )
  
  # Run the bootstrap samples in parallel
  ans <- parallel::mclapply(
    seq_len(R),
    function(i) {
      stat(dat[idx[, i], , drop = FALSE])
    },
    mc.cores = ncpus
  )
  
  # Convert the list into a matrix
  ans <- do.call(rbind, ans)
  
  return(ans)
}
```

```{r}
# Statistic calculated for each bootstrap sample
my_stat <- function(d) {
  coef(lm(y ~ x, data = d))
}

# Simulate data
set.seed(1)

n <- 500
R <- 1e4

x <- cbind(rnorm(n))
y <- x * 5 + rnorm(n)

dat <- data.frame(x, y)

# Parametric confidence intervals from lm()
ans0 <- confint(lm(y ~ x, data = dat))

# Bootstrap estimates using two cores
ans1 <- my_boot(
  dat = dat,
  stat = my_stat,
  R = R,
  ncpus = 2L
)

# Bootstrap confidence intervals
bootstrap_ci <- t(
  apply(ans1, 2, quantile, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
)

# Display both sets of confidence intervals
bootstrap_ci
ans0
```

The bootstrap and parametric confidence intervals from lm() should be very similar for both the intercepts and the x. Small differences are expected because the bootstrap CIs and parametric CIs are calculated using different methods.The former relies on assumptions  from a lm model whereas bootstrapping is based repeatedly resampling of data. 

```{r}
system.time(my_boot(dat = data.frame(x, y), my_stat, R = 4000, ncpus = 1L))
system.time(my_boot(dat = data.frame(x, y), my_stat, R = 4000, ncpus = 2L))
```
The 2 cores was faster than the 1 core as the elapsed time decreases from 2.971 seconds to 2.281 seconds, reducing by almost 0.69 seconds. The reported user time was also much lower for the 2 core run.
